strengths: First application of MeanFlow to text-to-audio generation, a novel and timely adaptation that eliminates the need for distillation teachers, unlike prior TTA acceleration approaches (ConsistencyTTA, AudioLCM, etc.)

The proposed instantaneous-to-mean curriculum with flow field mix-up is well-motivated and thoroughly ablated (Table 2, Table 3), clearly demonstrating that naive mean-flow training from scratch is unstable and that the curriculum improves both convergence speed and generation quality

Strong empirical results: MeanAudio achieves state-of-the-art single-step generation quality with a drastically smaller model (120M vs 500M-1250M parameters) and 100x speedup (RTF 0.013) over diffusion baselines, while remaining competitive in multi-step settings

Integration of CFG into the training target is a sound engineering contribution that avoids doubling NFE at inference, and the paper provides a careful ablation of guidance scale showing the expected quality/diversity trade-off

Reasonably thorough experimental section, comparing against multiple diffusion-based and distillation-based baselines under consistent metrics (FAD, FD, KL, IS, CLAP, RTF), with additional ablations isolating architecture design choices (mix-up ratio, CFG scale)

Practical relevance and reproducibility potential: authors state they will release code and weights, and provide enough algorithmic detail (Algorithms 1-2, hyperparameters) to attempt reimplementation
weaknesses: No human evaluation (e.g., MOS, perceptual quality, faithfulness) is reported; all results rely solely on automatic metrics (FAD, FD, KL, IS, CLAP), which are known to have limitations correlating with perceptual audio quality, especially for single-step/low-NFE generation where artifacts might not be captured
Evaluation is limited to a single dataset/benchmark (AudioCaps test set); no evaluation on Clotho, MusicCaps, or other TTA benchmarks to test generalization or robustness of the reported gains

Single random caption selection per test audio (out of 5 available) introduces variance that is not addressed via repeated runs/seeds or reported variance/confidence intervals, which could affect the reliability of the FD/FAD/CLAP comparisons, particularly given some improvements are of modest magnitude (e.g., a few percent) relative to baselines such as TangoFlux, GenAU

The proposed instantaneous-to-mean curriculum is closely related to existing methods (e.g., Flow-Anchored Consistency Models, cited as Peng et al. 2025) and MeanFlow itself (Geng et al. 2025), so the core novelty is primarily in adapting/combining known ideas for the audio domain rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic idea; the paper could more clearly delineate what is genuinely new vs. adapted

Ablations use "approximately 260 epochs" for fair comparison, but training budgets differ substantially across curriculum variants (96h vs 464h GPU-hours in Table 2), raising questions about whether comparisons are fully controlled for compute rather than epochs, particularly for the from-scratch MeanAudioMF baselines

Some overclaiming/vague language in the abstract/intro (e.g., "100x speedup" is compared against a specific 200-step baseline rather than a fair minimal-quality NFE baseline for competing methods, and choice of GenAU as the reference for the 100x figure is somewhat selective since faster diffusion baselines like TangoFlux exist)

Architecture and design choices (ConvMLP, RoPE, RMSNorm, dual FLAN-T5/CLAP conditioning) are adopted largely from prior work without individual ablation, making it hard to isolate how much of the final performance stems from the MeanFlow curriculum versus these architectural improvements

No discussion of failure cases, limitations of the single-step model (e.g., degraded generation for complex/multi-event captions), or computational cost/complexity of JVP computation during training relative to standard flow matching

strengths: First application of the MeanFlow objective to text-to-audio generation, achieving single-step (1-NFE) generation with strong quality, and demonstrating a real, substantial speedup (RTF 0.013) over prior diffusion/flow TTA baselines while using far fewer parameters (120M vs. 500M-1.4B).

Comprehensive empirical validation: objective metrics (FAD/FD/KL/IS/CLAP) across multiple NFE settings, a subjective human listening study (OVL/REL), and additional experiments on data/model scaling and music generation (MusicCaps), lending good support to the central claims.

Thorough and well-organized ablation studies isolating the contributions of the instantaneous-to-mean curriculum, the flow mix-up ratio, architectural components (CLAP, RoPE, ConvMLP), and the integrated CFG mechanism, which helps identify practical best practices and supports reproducibility.

The integration of CFG directly into the training target to avoid doubling NFE at inference is a sensible and effective engineering contribution specific to the mean-flow/audio setting, and the diagnosis of instability in naive MeanFlow training (with a proposed curriculum fix) is a useful practical finding for the field.
The paper provides sufficient implementation detail (architecture dimensions, training schedule, hyperparameters, datasets) and promises code/weight release, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The core generative objective (MeanFlow) is directly adopted from prior vision work (Geng et al., 2025); the paper's novelty lies mainly in engineering adaptations (curriculum, integrated CFG, architecture choices) rather than a fundamentally new modeling idea, which somewhat limits the conceptual contribution.

Baseline comparisons mix re-evaluated open-source checkpoints with numbers transcribed directly from other papers (marked with different symbols in Table 1/9), which can introduce inconsistencies in evaluation protocol (e.g., differing test conditions, caption selection) and complicate fair comparison.

The human subjective evaluation is relatively small in scale (10 experts rating only 10 samples per condition in the main study, 3 listeners on 10 captions in the dual-encoder study), and no statistical significance testing or confidence-interval analysis is reported, limiting the strength of claims drawn from these results.

The architectural design (Flux-style MMDiT with dual text encoders) closely follows existing designs (e.g., TangoFlux, Stable Audio), so the 'enhanced transformer' contribution is largely a combination of known techniques (RoPE, RMSNorm, SwiGLU, ConvMLP) rather than a novel architecture.

Evaluation is confined to short (10s) generic sound/music clips from AudioCaps/MusicCaps; broader claims about general TTA efficiency and quality would benefit from testing on more diverse or longer-form benchmarks, and the paper's own limitations section acknowledges these scope constraints.

strengths: Strong, well-validated empirical results: MeanAudio achieves SOTA single-step (1-NFE) text-to-audio generation quality (FD, KL, IS, CLAP) while using far fewer parameters (120M) than competing systems (500M-1.5B), with a 100x inference speedup (RTF 0.013) over strong diffusion baselines like GenAU.

Comprehensive and well-designed ablation studies (Tables 3-6) that isolate the contributions of the instantaneous-to-mean curriculum, flow mix-up ratio, architectural components (CLAP, RoPE, ConvMLP), and integrated CFG, providing genuinely useful practical guidance for building MeanFlow-based generators.
Both objective (FD/FAD/KL/IS/CLAP) and subjective (human OVL/REL) evaluations are reported and align well, strengthening the credibility of the quality claims.

Practical/engineering contribution: the model trains in ~3 days on 4 consumer RTX 3090 GPUs, which lowers the barrier for reproducing and extending this line of work; the authors commit to releasing code and weights.

Additional analyses (data/model scaling in Appendix C.2, MusicCaps music generation in Appendix C.3, detailed human eval of dual-text-encoder design in Appendix C.1) go beyond the minimum needed to support the core claims and show the approach is reasonably robust and extensible.
Clear exposition of the MeanFlow background, integrated CFG derivation, and training/inference algorithms, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is largely an adaptation of an existing method (MeanFlow, Geng et al. 2025) and existing architectural components (Flux-style MMDiT, dual FLAN-T5/CLAP conditioning used in prior TTA work) to a new domain; the main novel element is the instantaneous-to-mean curriculum with flow mix-up, which is a reasonable but incremental training-schedule innovation rather than a fundamentally new modeling idea.

Ablation studies are conducted with models trained from scratch on AudioCaps alone for 200k steps rather than using the full training pipeline (pretraining + fine-tuning) used for the main results, which may limit how directly ablation conclusions transfer to the full/best-performing model.

Primary quantitative evaluation relies heavily on a single benchmark (AudioCaps); while MusicCaps results are included as a secondary check in the appendix, broader domain diversity (e.g., sound effects only, diverse acoustic scenes) is not extensively tested.

Claims about the computational expense of distillation-based competitors (holding 2-3 models in memory, large offline trajectory storage) are stated but not directly quantified against MeanAudio's own training cost/memory footprint for a fully controlled comparison.

The model is restricted to fixed/short (10s) audio segments; the limitations section acknowledges this but the paper does not explore or discuss how this constrains real-world sound design applications where longer or variable-length generation matters.

The term "faithful" in the title/framing is not formally defined beyond standard alignment metrics (CLAP, REL), leaving the qualitative meaning somewhat vague relative to the strong claims made in the abstract/intro.
